content.thinking:
I need to plan out the battle axe design carefully, deciding how it should be displayed to touch the floor—either standing upright with its pommel resting on a small plinth, or lying flat.

I'll go with upright on an octagonal plinth base about 0.06m tall, total height roughly 1.05m, with the haft vertical and head at the top for a clean camera read. Since it's a plain object with no moving parts, I just need one root joint to anchor everything, with the blade profile in the XY plane extending toward +X and thickness along Z.

Now I'm sketching dimensions: the plinth as a lathed octagon with a stone-dark color, surrounded by icy cone shards at the base, the haft as a tapering swept shape with slight curvature and wood-grain coloring, and the blade head positioned near the top with the blade extending outward. Starting on the leather wrap detail next.

Adding the leather wrap and ring collars...

The pommel finishes as a faceted lathe shape in steel with diamond studs front and back, then I'm building the head socket as a beveled box around the haft with a crystal top cap surrounded by steel prongs, plus a backward-pointing spike cone for the reference axe-head detail.

Now I'm sketching the blade geometry itself—laying out the steel plate outline as a sequence of points extending from the socket out to a sharp upper horn and a sharp lower tip, with the ice edge extruded as a larger underlying shape and runes carved into the steel surface.

Continuing the outline down through the right side and back to the bottom-left, confirming the path moves clockwise without crossing itself—faceted with no smoothing to keep the low-poly style safe. Now I'm thinking about the ice edge as a separate, larger jagged crystalline shape extending outward past the steel blade.

Tracing through the full jagged chain of coordinates to confirm the edges don't cross each other before moving to the ice texture.

Making ice thicker than steel with a beveled edge, and considering adding a few stretched octahedron ice crystal spikes along the edge for extra detail. Working out a color gradient for the ice using mottled blues that lighten toward the outer edge.

For glowing elements, I'll create separate thin rune decal planes textured with cyan runes on a transparent background, placed just in front of and behind the steel core so the glow only shows where the runes are drawn, keeping everything else transparent.

For the steel body itself, I'm considering a mottled blue-grey cel paint plus a layered inset plate — a smaller, slightly thicker darker blue-grey extrusion scaled down from the main shape — to mimic the layered trim look from the reference design.

Working out inner outline coordinates, checking each point falls inside the steel edge boundary...

I need to figure out which side of this concave bottom edge counts as interior, checking the tip and adjacent points to make sure my chosen inner coordinate sits just inside the boundary rather than crossing it.

Still refining inner boundary coordinates...

I'm positioning the glow plane and front/back rune faces, then setting up the frame origins for the blade and haft, with the socket box sized to overlap the blade start and the steel band flanges on the lathe geometry.

Now I'm defining the top and bottom flange profiles for the lathe spin, placing studs as flattened octahedrons on the front and back faces, and adding side plates and spikes along the socket's sides.

For the crystal topper, I'm shaping it from a stretched octahedron with four angled prongs cradling it, making sure the haft terminates cleanly beneath the cap, and giving the crystal a flat pale-cyan glow with no bloom.

I'm also adding small hanging details—a thin cord looping off the haft with a tiny glowing ice shard dangling at the end—plus a ring of elongated octahedra scattered around the plinth as decorative ice shards.

I'm also thinking about carving faint glowing rune markings onto the haft's surface, placing them as a textured panel along one flat face between the wrapped grip sections, with a soft cyan glow to give it that enchanted weapon feel.

For the haft itself, I want to keep it straight so the rune panel stays flush, using a slight radius taper array to give it a subtle swelling profile rather than a perfectly uniform cylinder. I'm adjusting the panel's z-offset so it sits just outside the haft surface without floating or clipping into the wood.

Now I'm setting up the wood material with a cel-shaded grain texture pattern running along the y-axis for a natural carved look.

For the leather wrap I'm defining two cel-shaded brown tones, and for the steel parts I'm using mottled gray-blue cel shading with darker variants for shadowed areas. I'm also adding thin gold trim bands near the pommel and socket edges to give a touch of saturated accent color without overdoing it.

Now I'm skipping an edge-highlight strip on the blade and instead building the ice material using a gradient paint between pale blue tones, layered with a subtle white mottled noise for texture and nested inside the cel shader for lighting.

For the ice facets, since all extruded faces point the same direction they'll shade uniformly except for the beveled rim, so I'm adding small flat-shaded cone or tetrahedron shards stuck onto the ice surface—tilting them outward and placing roughly ten along both sides of the ice outline with slight offsets in depth to break up the flatness.

Placing a frost-crack texture plane over the ice region, sized and positioned to sit just above the ice surface without clipping into the inner steel layer, matching their half-thicknesses closely.

Now I'm sketching coordinates for the rune plate, mapping its SVG viewBox to the blade's inner dark plate region so the glyphs align within the blade's bounds.

Writing rune glyph paths...

I'm also setting up mirrored runes for the back-facing plane and starting the crack texture's viewBox dimensions for the next decorative plane.

Working out the texture coloring and glow import, then sketching the mace geometry: the plinth, the inverted-pyramid pommel resting on it, and the haft with rings running down its length.

Mapping out the ring and wrap positions along the haft, placing a leather wrap band, a ring, a runes section, and the socket flange, while keeping ring radii slightly larger than the haft so they read correctly.

Still writing geometry...

Still defining the geometry helpers...

Adding glow ring geometry...

I'm sizing the plinth radius and segment count, then checking the total figure height from plinth to crystal top stays sensible with the floor at zero. Now I'm working out a hanging charm detail—a curved leather cord suspending a small faceted shard from a ring partway up the structure.

For the final touches I'm making sure the cord and spiral wrap don't collide geometrically, adding metadata (name, description, style, commit hash) for the default export, and setting glow and texture options per part—using flat colors or texture maps, with proper direction and axis settings for front/back planes.

I'm refining the ice edge thickness and bevel values against the steel body and inner layer dimensions, checking the outline positioning relative to the extrusion origin, and deciding to skip an extra ice crown detail since the shards already cover that area. Now I'm starting on the gold trim lathe rings and a side block component.

Still writing side block and spike geometry...

I'm defining the four symmetrical prong spikes around the top, placing their base and tip positions using cosine and sine around a circle with steel coloring, then double-checking which imports I actually need -- confirming gradient is used for ice, paint for leather, and catmull for the cord path.

Now I need to fix a type error where mixed literal arrays infer incorrectly; I'll annotate outline arrays explicitly as OutlinePoint[] imported from the builder module, and define a typed helper variable for the reused lathe flange outline.
